newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: Portuguese archbishop installs new E.Timor bishop.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese archbishop installs new E.Timor bishop.

text.p: A Portuguese archbishop installed a new Catholic bishop in East Timor on Wednesday, reinforcing the role of the church as a peace broker in the troubled territory annexed by Indonesia two decades ago.

The Vatican, in a message read out at the colourful ceremony, said Pope John Paul hoped "a broad and truly just internationally accepted solution will be found to the complex and painful question of East Timor..."

Maurilio Gouveia, archbishop of Evera in Portugal, presided over the installation of Basilio do Nascimento, 46, as bishop of the newly formed diocese of Baucau, at the eastern end of Timor island. A choir sang in the local tetum dialect.
Papal Nuncio (ambassador) Pietro Sambi, who was due to have read out the Vatican's message, was taken ill on Tuesday night and returned to the territory's capital, Dili, before the ceremony.

The spotlight is on East Timor over the next few days with the installation of the new bishop as apostolic administrator, and visits by a senior U.S. human rights official and the new U.N. special envoy for East Timor.

Church sources said Gouveia had served in East Timor in the past, although they could not give the dates. Political analysts in Jakarta said the use of an archbishop from Portugal for the ceremony was likely to raise eyebrows in Jakarta.

Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 after civil war erupted following the withdrawal of Portuguese colonial authorities. Jakarta incorporated it as Indonesia's 27th province in 1976 in a move not recognised by the United Nations.
Indonesia and Portugal have been at loggerheads over the issue, and the new U.N. envoy for East Timor Jamsheed Marker is due to visit the territory at the weekend on a familiarisation trip.
About 20,000 people gathered under a sweltering morning sun in the main square of Baucau, a small town nestled between the sea and hills on the eastern flank of Timor island.
Church workers wearing distinctive black t-shirts controlled the crowd and no trouble was reported. There were no troops in sight and police kept a discreet distance.
"Up to now, everything has gone ahead smoothly. There have been no problems," East Timor's deputy police chief, Colonel Atok Rismanto, told Reuters from Dili.

Do Nascimento joins popular Bishop Carlos Belo, recipient of the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize for his work in East Timor, as the second bishop in the territory which the pope split into two dioceses late last year.
"East Timor...in the midst of tensions, the people await a response to their legitimate aspirations for the recognition of their specific culture and religious identity," the Vatican message said.

Do Nascimento, speaking at a mass following his installation at the lone church in Baucau, did not refer directly to the troubles in the area. But he said: "The church needs your help, even though you have problems of your own. I ask you to be courageous."
He also praised Belo, who had returned to Dili with the ill papal nuncio, saying "his courage is needed to strengthen the church in East Timor".
The territory's 850,000 people are mainly Roman Catholic in a nation of 200 million, of which more than 80 percent are Moslems.
